title: 10 — Design a Notification System
html:
10 — Design a Notification System

The one idea: decouple "something happened" from "a message was delivered". Services publish notification requests; a notification service validates, applies user preferences and rate limits, and puts one message per channel on its own queue; channel workers call the third-party providers with retries and idempotency.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Channels: push (iOS/Android), SMS, email.
  • Soft real-time: delivered quickly, slight delay under load is acceptable.
  • Devices: iOS, Android, desktop.
  • Triggered by client apps and by server-side schedules.
  • Users can opt out per channel.
  • Scale: 10M push, 1M SMS, 5M email per day.

Step 2 — High-level design

Channel mechanics

Channel Provider What you need
iOS push APNs Device token + payload
Android push Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) Registration token + payload
SMS Twilio, Azure Communication Services… Phone number
Email SendGrid, Mailgun, Azure Communication Services Email… Email address, templates

Contact info gathering

On install or sign-up, the API stores the device token / phone / email: user(id, email, phone), device(id, user_id, token, platform, last_seen).

The naive design and why it fails

One notification server calling all providers directly: SPOF, hard to scale each channel independently, and a slow provider stalls everything.

The improved design

---
title: Notification system — high-level architecture
---
flowchart LR
    S1["Service 1..N<br/>(billing, shipping…)"] --> NS["Notification servers<br/>(auth, validate, rate limit)"]
    NS --> Cache[("Cache<br/>user info, prefs, templates")]
    NS --> DB[("DB<br/>users, devices, settings, log")]
    NS --> Qi["iOS queue"]
    NS --> Qa["Android queue"]
    NS --> Qs["SMS queue"]
    NS --> Qe["Email queue"]
    Qi --> Wi["Workers"] --> APNs["APNs"]
    Qa --> Wa["Workers"] --> FCM["FCM"]
    Qs --> Ws["Workers"] --> SMS["SMS provider"]
    Qe --> We["Workers"] --> EM["Email provider"]
  • One queue per channel — an outage at one provider only backs up its queue.
  • Notification servers are stateless and horizontally scaled.
  • Workers scale independently per channel.

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Reliability — no lost notifications

  • Persist a notification log before enqueueing; workers update status (queued → sent → delivered/failed).
  • Queues are durable; workers ack only after the provider accepts.
  • Retries with exponential backoff; after N failures → dead-letter queue + alert.

3.2 Exactly-once? No — at-least-once plus dedupe

Queues deliver at least once, so duplicates happen. Give each notification an event ID; workers check "already sent?" (DB or Redis SETNX with TTL) before calling the provider.

3.3 Extra components

Component Why
Templates Consistent formatting, localisation, fewer bugs; parameters filled at send time
Settings (user_id, channel, opt_in) checked before enqueueing
Rate limiting Cap notifications per user per day — too many and users disable them entirely
Security Only authenticated services (appKey/appSecret or managed identity) may send
Monitoring Queue depth per channel is the key metric — growing depth → add workers
Event tracking Open / click / delivery events for analytics (→ chapter 21)

3.4 Priorities and scheduling

  • Separate high-priority queues (OTP, security alerts) from bulk marketing so a campaign never delays a login code.
  • Scheduled sends: store with send_at, a scheduler enqueues when due; respect quiet hours in the user's timezone.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Talking points: reliability via persistence + retries, dedupe for at-least-once, per-channel isolation, user preferences, rate limits, templates, monitoring, and priority lanes.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Azure Notification Hubs — fan-out to APNs/FCM/WNS with tags (e.g. user:123), handles device registration.
  • Azure Communication Services — SMS and Email with delivery reports via Event Grid.
  • Service Bus — one queue (or topic subscription) per channel; built-in duplicate detection window by MessageId; scheduled messages (ScheduledEnqueueTime) for delayed sends; DLQ for poison messages.
  • Workers: BackgroundService with ServiceBusProcessor, or Azure Functions with Service Bus triggers.
  • Templates: Razor (RazorLight) or Scriban/Liquid for email bodies.
  • Resilience: Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience for provider HTTP calls (retry + circuit breaker + timeout).
  • Transactional safety: outbox pattern — write the notification request in the same DB transaction as the business change, then publish.

Review checklist

  • Channels and providers named.
  • Queue per channel; stateless notification servers.
  • Persistence + retries + DLQ → no loss.
  • Idempotency/dedupe for at-least-once.
  • Preferences, rate limits, templates, priority lanes.
  • Queue depth as the scaling signal.
